stories.source_title: Four T. rex footprints hint at how fast it traveled
stories.excerpt:
Four fossilized footprints are helping scientists step into a dinosaur’s shoes. The prints form the first known set of tracks likely left by an adult Tyrannosaurus rex.

A trackway is three or more consecutive footprints left by some animal. The one for this T. rex spans 7 meters (10 feet). The track spacing suggests the ancient predator had been ambling along at about 1.6 meters (5.2 feet) per second, which would be a quick walking pace for us.

story.title: T. rex footprints show its walking speed
story.teaser: Four giant footprints reveal how fast a T. rex walked
body: Scientists have studied four fossil footprints that were probably left by an adult Tyrannosaurus rex. They are the first known trackway from a grown-up T. rex.

The trackway stretches 7 metres. By measuring the gaps between the prints, the team worked out that the dinosaur was walking at about 1.6 metres per second. That is about as fast as a person walking quickly.

Kent Hups, a teacher and fossil hunter, found the prints in North Dakota. The first one had three toes and was huge, measuring 80 centimetres across. The prints were made roughly 66.5 million years ago.
Peter Falkingham from Liverpool John Moores University helped study them. He said one footprint does not tell you much, but a trackway shows how an animal moves.
A fifth footprint may be hidden in the hill. The team is waiting for nature to wear the rock away.

word_to_know.definition: A line of three or more footprints left by an animal as it moves along.

body: Wales manager Craig Bellamy has praised Liverpool for the way they have looked after young forward Lewis Koumas.
Koumas is 21 years old. He spent time on loan at football clubs in the Championship, including Stoke City and Hull City. He helped Hull City move up to the Premier League.

story.title: Arsenal take on mighty Barcelona
story.teaser: How do Barcelona keep winning when big stars leave?
body: Arsenal are playing Barcelona in the Women's Champions League on Thursday. The match is at the Nou Camp, Barcelona's famous stadium.

Barcelona are the champions. They have won four of the past six Women's Champions League titles. Some big stars left the club in the summer. But the team has still won all three of its matches so far, scoring 19 goals.

So how do they do it? Many of their players learn the game at La Masia, the club's famous academy. Young players there are all trained to play the same way. They learn to swap positions easily. Star player Aitana Bonmati learned there.
Barcelona's passing style is called tiki-taka. Player Esmee Brugts said the secret is "doing the simple things good".
Arsenal have made a good start in Europe too, with seven points from their first three matches. They beat Barcelona in the 2025 final, so it should be an exciting game.

story.title: Teen steers robot through kelp forests
story.teaser: Why are some underwater forests growing back?
body: Linden Hunter-Pinsky, 14, lives by the ocean in Santa Cruz, California. He steered an underwater robot to find out why some kelp forests are growing back while others are shrinking.
California's kelp shrank a lot in the 2010s, partly because of a heat wave. Linden wondered if the beds that were recovering had fewer sea urchins, which munch on kelp.

He used satellite data to choose kelp beds that were shrinking, growing back or staying the same. Then he and his dad rowed out in their family rowboat, because a motor could get caught in the kelp. Linden got seasick, but he loved watching fish swim past on the robot's video.

The video showed hardly any sea urchins anywhere. So Linden thinks other things, such as runoff, matter more. Kelp forests are home to many creatures and protect the shore from erosion, so learning how they thrive is important.

story.title: Arctic air brings a sudden chill to UK
story.teaser: Find out why the big coats are back out
body: The UK has suddenly turned very cold. A blast of icy air from the Arctic has moved down towards the country. In some country areas of England, night-time temperatures were expected to fall to -5C.
Many people have spotted frost on grass, cars and pavements. Some parts of Northern Scotland could even see light flurries of snow.

Weather like this is sometimes caused by a polar vortex. This is a huge area of very cold air that spins high up around the North Pole. Usually, strong winds keep it locked in place. But if those winds weaken, some of the cold air can escape south.
Experts at the Met Office say it is very early in the year for this to happen. Scientist Jeff Knight said it seems to be the earliest on record in the 75 years they have been watching.
But this does not mean lots of snow is coming. By the weekend, milder weather is set to arrive from the Atlantic Ocean.

word_to_know.definition: A giant swirl of very cold air that spins high above the North Pole.

story.title: Why has it turned so cold so suddenly?
story.teaser: A blast of Arctic air has made the UK chilly. Here's why.
body: A blast of Arctic air has moved down towards the UK. The temperature has dropped fast. In some country areas of England, nights could get as cold as -5C.
You may have spotted frost on grass, cars and pavements. Some parts of Northern Scotland could even see light flurries of snow.

Sometimes this kind of weather is linked to a polar vortex. This is a huge area of very cold air that spins high up around the North Pole. Powerful winds usually keep it in place. Sometimes those winds weaken, and cold air can escape southwards.

The Met Office says it is very early in the year for this to happen. Experts say it is a very unusual event. But it does not mean lots of snow is on the way. By the weekend, milder weather will arrive from the Atlantic Ocean.

word_to_know.definition: A huge area of very cold air that spins high up above the North Pole.

story.think_about_it: What clothes would you pick for a frosty morning, and why?

story.title: A blast of Arctic air has arrived
story.teaser: Brrr! Find out why the UK suddenly feels freezing.
body: Wrap up warm! A blast of freezing Arctic air has swept down towards the UK, making temperatures drop suddenly. Some rural parts of England could see temperatures fall to -5C overnight, with frost on grass, cars and pavements.

The chilly weather is linked to something called a polar vortex. That is a huge area of very cold air that spins high above the North Pole. Strong winds usually keep it locked in place, but sometimes those winds weaken. When that happens, cold air can escape south towards places that are normally milder, like the UK.
Experts at the Met Office say it is very early in the year for this to happen. Climate scientist Jeff Knight said it looks like the earliest event of its kind in 75 years of records.
Don't put away your lighter coats yet, though. By the weekend, milder weather will arrive from the Atlantic Ocean, and experts say this does not mean lots of snow is on the way.

word_to_know.definition: A swirling mass of air or water that spins around like a whirlpool.

story.think_about_it: What signs of winter weather have you spotted near you, like frost or fog?

story.title: Why has it suddenly got so cold?
story.teaser: A polar vortex is sending icy Arctic air towards the UK.
body: Have you dug out your biggest coat this week? A blast of Arctic air has moved down towards the UK, making it suddenly very cold. Overnight temperatures may fall to -5C in rural spots.
You may have seen frost on grass, cars and pavements. Parts of Northern Scotland could even see light flurries of snow.
This chilly weather can be caused by a polar vortex. That is a huge area of very cold air spinning high up in the atmosphere around the North Pole.
Most of the time, strong winds keep it locked in place. If those winds weaken, cold Arctic air can escape southwards towards places like the UK.

Met Office experts say this is very early for it to happen. Lead climate scientist Jeff Knight said it looks like the earliest on record over 75 years. Milder weather will arrive from the Atlantic Ocean, so don't put away lighter coats yet.

word_to_know.definition: A huge spinning area of very cold air high above the North Pole.

The source only says weather like this is 'sometimes' caused by a polar vortex, and it warns that not every chilly spell is caused by one. It never directly says this cold snap comes from the polar vortex.
